parts.title: Booking a vineyard tour
parts.context: A man books a tour and wine tasting for a company outing.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a vineyard to book a tour for his colleagues. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: Hillside Vineyard, Ms Marsh speaking.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a tour and a wine tasting for a group. It's a company outing, to thank my colleagues for a good year.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: What a nice idea. I'll take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The booking is for a company outing, so 'outing' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: robert
script.text: Robert Whitfield. That's W-H-I-T-F-I-E-L-D.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: Thank you, Mr Whitfield. How many people will be in the group?

script.speaker: robert
script.text: Twenty. We had twenty-five at first, but a few can't come.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: And which date would you like?

script.speaker: robert
script.text: Saturday the eleventh of October, if that's possible.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: It is. Tours normally start at eleven in the winter, but in October we begin at ten, so you'll be here before it gets busy.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: That's perfect.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: The tour is about an hour and a half, followed by a tasting of five wines.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: Only five? I was expecting more.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: Five is what most people can cope with, believe me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: The price is eighteen pounds per person. It was twenty-two last year, but we've introduced a reduction for groups of fifteen or more.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: That's good value. Is food included?

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: Yes, there's a lunch after the tasting, a platter with bread, cheese and cold meat, and a glass of grape juice for anyone who doesn't drink.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: Our colleagues are coming by train. Is the vineyard easy to reach?

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: We'll send our minibus to collect everyone from the station, and take them back afterwards, so there's no need to arrange taxis.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: That's very helpful. Is there anything people should bring?

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: Warm clothes, because the cellars are cold, even in summer. And please tell them to wear flat shoes, as there are steps.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: And can we buy wine to take home?

script.speaker: marsh
script.text: Of course. There's a ten percent discount on everything in the shop for tour groups.

script.speaker: robert
script.text: Excellent. I'll confirm the booking this afternoon.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Volunteering at a hospital
parts.context: A coordinator briefs new hospital volunteers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator briefing new volunteers at a hospital. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: Welcome, everybody, and thank you for volunteering at St Anne's Hospital. I'm Funmi Adeyemi, the volunteer coordinator. I'll begin by explaining where each role is based, because people often get lost on their first day.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: If you're welcoming visitors, you'll be at the main entrance. Your job is to greet people, answer their questions, and walk with them to the right department if they need it.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: Anyone who likes children might prefer the children's ward, where volunteers read stories, play games, and keep the little patients company while their parents have a break.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: In the outpatients waiting area, volunteers serve tea and biscuits to patients who sometimes have to wait for hours. A cup of tea makes a big difference.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: If you enjoy plants, there's a job in the garden, which patients use for gentle walks and where people sit with visitors. The gardeners could always use more help.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: And we have a gift shop, run entirely by volunteers, which sells cards and small presents. All the profits go to buy equipment for the wards. The chapel and the pharmacy don't use volunteers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: A few facts. The hospital has about three hundred and fifty volunteers, which is fewer than we need, so you're very welcome.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: We ask you to give at least four hours a week. Most people give more, once they've started, but we don't want anyone to feel under pressure.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: Before you begin, everyone has a background check, which is a legal requirement because you'll be working with vulnerable people. It takes about two weeks, so you can't start until it's complete.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: There's no uniform. You wear your own clothes, but you do need a badge, which you'll collect today, and you must keep it visible at all times.

script.speaker: adeyemi
script.text: And as a thank you, volunteers get a free lunch in the staff canteen on the days they work. Now, if you'll follow me, I'll take you to collect your badges.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Nursing placements
parts.context: Two nursing students compare their placements.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two nursing students, Abby and Femi, discussing their clinical placements. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: abby
script.text: Femi, how was your placement on the surgical ward? Mine was on the children's ward, and it was much harder than I'd imagined.

script.speaker: femi
script.text: Mine was tiring but good. What was the hardest thing for you?

script.speaker: abby
script.text: Talking to worried parents. I never knew what to say, and I was afraid of saying something wrong.

script.speaker: femi
script.text: How did you cope?

script.speaker: abby
script.text: My mentor told me that listening is more important than talking, so I just listened, and it helped a lot.

script.speaker: femi
script.text: On my ward, the hardest thing was the pace. Twelve-hour shifts, and sometimes no break at all.

script.speaker: abby
script.text: What did you learn about teamwork?

script.speaker: femi
script.text: That the nursing assistants know a huge amount. At first I ignored them, but they taught me how to move patients safely.

script.speaker: abby
script.text: Did you make any mistakes?

script.speaker: femi
script.text: One. I gave a patient the wrong form to sign. It wasn't serious, but I reported it at once, and my mentor praised me for that.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: femi
script.text: And what skills do you think you developed?

script.speaker: abby
script.text: My communication, definitely, and I'm much better at managing my time, because on the ward there were so many things to do at once. I can't say the same for the equipment. I'm still nervous with the machines.

script.speaker: femi
script.text: That will come with practice. What happens next term for you?

script.speaker: abby
script.text: I have a placement in a community clinic, which is quite different, with fewer emergencies and more talking to patients.

script.speaker: femi
script.text: I'd love that. I want to work in mental health in the end, so I'll try to get a placement like that too.

script.speaker: abby
script.text: That's a really good aim. Are you going to the library this weekend? The reflective essay is due on Monday.

script.speaker: femi
script.text: Yes, let's go on Saturday morning and work on it together.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about hummingbirds. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Hummingbirds are some of the most extraordinary birds in the world. There are more than three hundred species, and every one of them lives in the Americas, from Alaska in the north to the southern tip of Chile.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: They are tiny. The smallest weighs less than a coin. But they are champions of flight. They beat their wings about fifty times a second, and they can hover in front of a flower, and they are the only birds that can fly backwards.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: All this effort needs a lot of energy. A hummingbird's heart can beat over a thousand times a minute, and the bird has to eat very often. It feeds on nectar, the sugary liquid in flowers, and it drinks many times its own weight in a day. Its long beak and a tongue that is almost as long as the beak reach deep inside the flower.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Nectar provides sugar, but not protein, so the birds also catch small insects, which they pick out of the air or from spiders' webs.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: How do they survive when they cannot feed, for example, at night? Some species solve the problem by lowering their body temperature, so that their heart rate and breathing slow down, and they use much less energy until morning.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Some hummingbirds also make remarkable journeys. The ruby-throated hummingbird, which weighs about as much as a coin, flies non-stop across the Gulf of Mexico on its migration, a journey of many hours, with no chance to rest or eat on the way.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: And a last curiosity: hummingbirds are strongly attracted to the colour red, which is why bird feeders for them are usually red. Gardeners who plant red flowers will soon get visitors. Next week we'll look at owls.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
